rationale: A wins because it knows where the floorboards are thin and says so before anyone falls through. Its strongest line, "confirmation there is genuinely no enterprise sales team (the fact block only says none is 'mentioned')," shows actual discipline; B's "It's Not Building a Sales Team to Do It" turns an absence in the brief into a headline. B has sharper copy, but some of that sharpness is just unsupported confidence wearing a nice jacket.
gaps_in_A: "Linear is selling to the enterprise without an enterprise sales team" overstates the brief. The update says no enterprise sales team is mentioned; it does not say Linear is selling to enterprise buyers or has no sales motion.
"contested ground the incumbents own" is plausible category context, but it is still asserted without evidence from the update.
"the slower, more visual, more collaborative way non-engineers work" risks stereotyping PMs and designers. The angle is good, but that claim needs user evidence or a customer quote, not vibes.
gaps_in_B: "It's Not Building a Sales Team to Do It" is too definitive. The supplied fact is only that no enterprise sales team is mentioned.
"every software company that successfully expands its addressable market deploys sales headcount and a demand-gen machine" is a fake law of SaaS physics. Too broad, too confident, and not needed.
"Productboard, Aha!, and Jira's PM-facing workflows" plus "complaints about bloat, slowness, and over-complexity" imports a whole competitive narrative not present in the update.
"Pick an angle, then go to meanest-editor" is the wrong next step. The useful next move is proof gathering and journalist fit, not sending the angles back through another critique loop.
